title: Handling Missing Data II - Numerical Imputation
abstract:
The four univariate techniques for numerical columns from the notes: mean/median
imputation, arbitrary value imputation, end-of-distribution imputation, and
random sample imputation. For each this document gives the rule, when to use it,
the exact damage it does to the distribution — with the variance-shrinkage
formula derived — and the missing-indicator trick that recovers most of what
imputation destroys. It closes with how to select among them by cross-validation
rather than by habit.

blocks.t: Mean / Median Imputation
From the notes
Impute missing values with mean/median.

items: Mean — use when the data is normal.
Median — use when the result is skewed.
Both are used when there are few missing values.

blocks.t: Disadvantage: the distribution changes, and it creates outliers.

blocks.cap:
A right-skewed column with 35% of values missing, treated five ways.
 Mean and median imputation both plant an enormous artificial spike at a single
 value and collapse the standard deviation. Random sample imputation is the only
 one that preserves the shape.

blocks.t: Why the distribution changes — the mathematics
Variance shrinkage, derived

Let a column have true mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, with a fraction $f$
of values missing completely at random. Replace every missing value by the
observed mean $\bar x \approx \mu$. The imputed column has $n(1-f)$ original
values and $nf$ copies of $\mu$.

The mean is unchanged:
$\mathbb{E}[x_{\text{imp}}] = (1-f)\mu + f\mu = \mu$.
The variance is not. The imputed values contribute zero deviation:

\operatorname{Var}(x_{\text{imp}})
 = \frac{1}{n}\Big[\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{\text{observed}}(x_i-\mu)^2}_{\approx n(1-f)\sigma^2}
 + \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{\text{imputed}}(\mu-\mu)^2}_{= 0}\Big]
 = (1-f) \sigma^{2}.
So
\boxed{ \sigma_{\text{imp}} = \sigma\sqrt{1-f} }

At $f=0.35$ the standard deviation falls to $\sqrt{0.65}=81\%$ of its true value.
At $f=0.50$ it falls to $71\%$.

blocks.cap:
Left: measured shrinkage matches $\sqrt{1-f}$ exactly. Middle: the
 imputed rows form a vertical stripe of fabricated points at the mean — these
 are the "created outliers" the notes warn about, and they are outliers in the
 joint distribution even though they sit at the centre of the marginal
 one. Right: every method attenuates the correlation with other columns.

blocks.t: Two consequences that matter downstream

1. Understated uncertainty. Standard errors, confidence intervals and
$p$-values computed on mean-imputed data are too narrow. The analysis is more
confident than the evidence warrants.

2. Attenuated correlations. Imputed points sit at the mean of one
variable while retaining their true value on the other, which pulls every
correlation towards zero. A genuinely predictive feature can be made to look
useless.
Mean or median — the actual rule

Use the median by default. It is robust to skew and to outliers, and it
never lands on a value that is impossible in the data (the mean of a count column
can be $2.7$ children). Use the mean only when you have checked that the column
is close to symmetric.
Arbitrary Value Imputation
From the notes
Used in categorical data mostly. The variants:

items: Impute with something that already does not exist

blocks.t:
For numerical columns, the value chosen is deliberately outside the real range
— $-1$, $-999$, $9999$. The point is that the model can recognise the
sentinel and learn a separate rule for it. Tree models do this well: a single
split at $x < 0$ isolates every imputed row.
Never use $0$ as the sentinel for a numeric column

$0$ is usually a legitimate value — zero income, zero purchases, zero days.
Imputing with $0$ makes "missing" indistinguishable from "genuinely zero",
which are entirely different facts. Choose a value that cannot occur, and
document it. And never feed a sentinel like $-999$ to a linear or distance-based
model: it is not a rule to that model, it is an enormous outlier that will
dominate every coefficient and distance.
End of Distribution Imputation
From the notes
Impute with:

We impute with the end of values. Used when data is not missing at
random.

blocks.cap:
Left: where the two formulas place the imputed value — the $3\sigma$
 rule for symmetric data, the IQR fence for skewed data. Right: why the method
 exists at all — when data is MNAR the fact of being missing carries signal,
 and pushing the value to the tail lets a tree isolate those rows.

blocks.t: Why the tail, and not the centre

This is the method for MNAR data (Topic 23), where missingness is
informative. Median imputation hides those rows in the middle of the
distribution, where they are indistinguishable from ordinary rows. Pushing them
to the tail marks them: a tree can isolate them with one split, and a linear
model gives them a distinctly different fitted value.

The $3\sigma$ and $1.5\,\text{IQR}$ choices are not arbitrary — they are exactly
the outlier fences of Topics 28–29. The method deliberately places imputed
values where genuine outliers would be, just past the bulk of the data.

The cost is that you are inventing extreme values. Variance is inflated rather
than shrunk, and any model sensitive to outliers — linear regression, KNN, SVM
— is badly served. Use it with tree-based models.
Random Sample Imputation
From the notes

items: Impute with a random number from the existing data.

blocks.t:
Draw each missing value at random from the observed values of the same column.
It is the only univariate method that preserves the distribution's shape,
variance and quantiles — as the first figure shows, its histogram is
indistinguishable from the original.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Preserves the distribution and the variance exactly
Not deterministic — two runs give different data
No artificial spike, no invented outliers
Still ignores the other columns, so it breaks correlations
Works for numerical and categorical alike
Requires storing the training pool for use at serving time

blocks.t: Non-determinism is a production problem

The same customer scored twice can get two different predictions. Fix it by
seeding the draw from a stable key — a hash of the customer ID — so the same
row always receives the same imputed value. Otherwise your model is not a
function.
The Missing Indicator
The single most valuable trick in this topic

Whatever you impute, add a binary column recording that the value was
missing. Imputation destroys the information "this was absent"; the indicator
gives it back. Under MAR and MNAR the indicator is frequently more predictive
than the imputed value itself, and it costs one column.

With the indicator present, a model can learn a separate effect for imputed rows
regardless of what value you filled in — which makes the choice of imputation
value much less critical.
Choosing Between Them
The notes' own advice: let cross-validation decide

The notes suggest using GridSearchCV to find the best params
(techniques). Imputation strategy is a hyperparameter. Put the imputer in a
pipeline (Topic 17) and search over strategy — this replaces an argument
about which method is "right" with a number.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer, MissingIndicator
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, FeatureUnion
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 6000
income = rng.lognormal(3.4, .65, n)                 # right-skewed
score  = 0.8 * np.log(income) + rng.normal(0, .35, n)
y = (0.9 * np.log(income) + 0.5 * score + rng.normal(0, 1, n) > 4.4).astype(int)

# MNAR: the highest earners decline to answer
missing = income > np.percentile(income, 68)
obs = income.copy(); obs[missing] = np.nan
df = pd.DataFrame({"income": obs, "score": score})
print(f"missing {np.isnan(obs).mean():.0%}")

# =====================================================================
# 1. MEAN / MEDIAN -- and the variance shrinkage, verified
# =====================================================================
mean_imp   = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()
median_imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()

f = np.isnan(obs).mean()
print(f"true std      {income.std():.2f}")
print(f"mean-imputed  {mean_imp.std():.2f}   theory sigma*sqrt(1-f) = "
      f"{np.nanstd(obs) * np.sqrt(1 - f):.2f}")
print(f"shrinkage factor observed {mean_imp.std()/income.std():.3f}  "
      f"predicted {np.sqrt(1-f):.3f}")

# The "creates outliers" problem is about the JOINT distribution:
r_true = np.corrcoef(np.log(income), score)[0, 1]
r_mean = np.corrcoef(np.log(mean_imp), score)[0, 1]
print(f"correlation with score:  true {r_true:.3f}   after mean imputation {r_mean:.3f}")
# Attenuated -- a real signal made to look weaker than it is.

# =====================================================================
# 2. ARBITRARY VALUE
# =====================================================================
arb = SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value=-999).fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()
print("sentinel rows:", (arb == -999).sum())

# WHY NOT ZERO: it collides with a legitimate value
counts = np.where(rng.random(n) < .2, 0, rng.poisson(3, n)).astype(float)
counts[rng.random(n) < .1] = np.nan
zero_imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value=0).fit_transform(
    counts.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()
print("rows that are now 0:", (zero_imp == 0).sum(),
      "-- genuinely zero AND missing, indistinguishable")

# =====================================================================
# 3. END OF DISTRIBUTION -- both formulas from the notes
# =====================================================================
class EndOfDistributionImputer(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """mu + 3*sigma for normal data;  Q3 + 1.5*IQR for skewed data."""
    def __init__(self, method="iqr", tail="right"):
        self.method, self.tail = method, tail
    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        v = X[~np.isnan(X)]
        if self.method == "gaussian":
            m, s = v.mean(), v.std()
            self.value_ = m + 3*s if self.tail == "right" else m - 3*s
        else:
            q1, q3 = np.nanpercentile(v, [25, 75]); iqr = q3 - q1
            self.value_ = q3 + 1.5*iqr if self.tail == "right" else q1 - 1.5*iqr
        return self
    def transform(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float).copy()
        X[np.isnan(X)] = self.value_
        return X

eod = EndOfDistributionImputer(method="iqr").fit(df[["income"]])
print(f"IQR fence      Q3+1.5IQR = {eod.value_:.2f}")
print(f"gaussian fence mu+3sigma = "
      f"{EndOfDistributionImputer(method='gaussian').fit(df[['income']]).value_:.2f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. RANDOM SAMPLE -- the only method that preserves the shape
# =====================================================================
class RandomSampleImputer(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Draw from the observed TRAINING values. Seeded per row for determinism."""
    def __init__(self, random_state=0):
        self.random_state = random_state
    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        self.pool_ = X[~np.isnan(X)]          # stored for use at SERVING time
        return self
    def transform(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float).copy()
        idx = np.isnan(X)
        if idx.any():
            r = np.random.default_rng(self.random_state)
            X[idx] = r.choice(self.pool_, idx.sum())
        return X

rs = RandomSampleImputer().fit_transform(df[["income"]]).ravel()
print(f"\nstd:      true {income.std():.2f}  mean-imp {mean_imp.std():.2f}  "
      f"random-sample {rs.std():.2f}")
print(f"skew:     true {pd.Series(income).skew():.2f}  "
      f"mean-imp {pd.Series(mean_imp).skew():.2f}  "
      f"random-sample {pd.Series(rs).skew():.2f}")
# Random sampling matches the original on BOTH moments. Nothing else does.

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE MISSING INDICATOR -- usually worth more than the imputed value
# =====================================================================
df["income_missing"] = df.income.isna().astype(int)
print("\ntarget rate | not missing:", y[df.income_missing == 0].mean().round(3))
print("target rate | missing    :", y[df.income_missing == 1].mean().round(3))
# Large gap => the ABSENCE is the signal. This is MNAR.

# sklearn does it for you:
imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True)
out = imp.fit_transform(df[["income"]])
print("columns out:", out.shape[1], "(value + indicator)")

# =====================================================================
# 6. COMPARE THEM ALL, PROPERLY -- inside cross-validation
# =====================================================================
X = df[["income", "score"]]

setups = {
    "mean":            SimpleImputer(strategy="mean"),
    "median":          SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
    "median + flag":   SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True),
    "arbitrary -999":  SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value=-999),
    "end of dist":     Pipeline([("e", EndOfDistributionImputer()),
                                 ("nothing", "passthrough")]),
    "random sample":   RandomSampleImputer(),
}
print(f"\n{'imputer':18s} {'LogReg':>9s} {'Forest':>9s}")
for name, tf in setups.items():
    lr = Pipeline([("imp", tf), ("sc", StandardScaler()),
                   ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    rf = Pipeline([("imp", tf),
                   ("m", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=150, random_state=0))])
    a = cross_val_score(lr, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
    b = cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
    print(f"{name:18s} {a:9.4f} {b:9.4f}")
# Note the pattern: "arbitrary -999" and "end of dist" are competitive for the
# FOREST and terrible for LOGISTIC REGRESSION -- exactly as the theory predicts.

# =====================================================================
# 7. LET GRIDSEARCH CHOOSE -- the notes' own advice
# =====================================================================
pipe = Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer()),
                 ("sc",  StandardScaler()),
                 ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, {
    "imp__strategy":      ["mean", "median", "most_frequent", "constant"],
    "imp__fill_value":    [0, -1, -999],
    "imp__add_indicator": [False, True],
    "clf__C":             [0.1, 1.0, 10.0],
}, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1, error_score="raise").fit(X, y)
print("\nbest imputation:", {k: v for k, v in gs.best_params_.items() if "imp" in k})
print("best cv auc:", round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# =====================================================================
# 8. FIT ON TRAIN ONLY -- the median is a learned parameter
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te = train_test_split(X, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit(X_tr)
print("\nmedian learned from TRAIN:", imp.statistics_.round(2))
X_te_i = imp.transform(X_te)                # reuses the TRAIN median
print("test median would have been:",
      np.nanmedian(X_te, axis=0).round(2), "-- NOT used, correctly")
Worked Examples
Mean versus median on a skewed column
Column income_k = $[1,\,2,\,3,\,4,\,100,\;\text{NaN}]$ (values in thousands). One value is missing.
Step 1 – compute the candidate fills from the observed values $[1,2,3,4,100]$:
\text{mean} = \frac{110}{5} = 22, \qquad \text{median} = 3

Step 2 – compare. Imputing with the mean sets the missing value to $22$. That number is above four of the five observed incomes and sits in a region where no real data exists. The median $3$ represents the typical value.

Step 3 – what each choice does to the distribution. Adding a point at 22 shifts the mean of the completed column to $132/6 = 22$ (unchanged, by construction) but shrinks the variance. Repeating this for many missing values concentrates mass artificially at the mean.
Rule of thumb. Symmetric column (for example $[10,20,30,40,50]$, mean $=$ median $=30$): mean is fine. Skewed column: median.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Mean/median imputation. Mean when the data is normal, median
 when the result is skewed. Both used when there are few missing
 values. Disadvantage: the distribution changes and it creates
 outliers.

Variance shrinks by exactly $\sqrt{1-f}$ where $f$ is the missing
 fraction. Correlations are attenuated. Standard errors become too narrow.

Arbitrary value imputation — mostly for categorical data:
 the word "Missing", $0$ or $-1$, or something that already does not
 exist. Never use $0$ for a numeric column — it collides with
 genuine zeros.

End of distribution imputation. Normal data:
 $\mu\pm3\sigma$. Skewed data: $Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR}$ or
 $Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}$. Used when data is not missing at random.
 Trees only.

Random sample imputation — impute with a random number drawn
 from the existing data. Keeps the distribution intact. Seed it
 per row so it is deterministic.

Always add a missing indicator. Under MAR and MNAR it is often
 more predictive than the value you imputed.

Imputation strategy is a hyperparameter — use GridSearchCV to
 find the best technique rather than arguing about it.
The imputation statistic is learned: fit on train only.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What is wrong with mean imputation?

It shrinks the variance by $\sqrt{1-f}$, plants an artificial spike at a single
value, attenuates correlations with other columns, and understates uncertainty in
any downstream inference. It is acceptable only when very little is missing.
Q. Mean or median?

Median by default — robust to skew and outliers, and it always lands on a
plausible value. Use the mean only after checking that the column is close to
symmetric.
Q. When would you deliberately impute with an extreme value?

When the data is MNAR and you are using a tree-based model. Pushing the imputed
rows to the tail lets the tree isolate them with a single split, so it can learn a
separate rule for "this was missing". Never do it for a linear or
distance-based model — it becomes a dominating outlier.
Q. Which imputation method preserves the distribution?

Random sample imputation — drawing from the observed values of the same column.
It preserves the shape, the variance and the quantiles. Its drawback is
non-determinism, which you fix by seeding from a stable row key.
Q. Why add a missing indicator?

Because imputation destroys the information that the value was absent, and that
absence is frequently predictive — under MNAR it can be the strongest signal in
the column. It costs one binary feature and lets the model learn a separate
effect for imputed rows.
Q. Why is imputing a numeric column with 0 dangerous?

Zero is usually a legitimate value. After imputation you cannot distinguish
"no purchases" from "we do not know", and the model learns a blended,
incorrect effect for both.
